outcome: The Riemann hypothesis is unproven as of 13 October 2026, but since 26 January 2024 it has seen partial, proportion-type movement: an unconditional lower bound that at least two-thirds of nontrivial zeros in windows [T,2T] are simple and on the critical line, credited to an unreleased Claude research model and verified by Anthropic staff (August 2026), a shorter human re-proof of a 67.25% version (Lamzouri, September 2026), and an unreviewed OpenAI claim of a zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for zeta and all Dirichlet L-functions (October 2026); alongside these, many self-published claims of a full proof or disproof, none accepted.
problem_asks: (1) That every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s), i.e. every zero with 0 < Re s < 1, has real part exactly 1/2, so that it lies on the critical line 1/2 + it with t real. (2) Stated as a single yes-or-no question about all nontrivial zeros together; it is universal over zeros. It does not ask for proportions, counts, simplicity of zeros, zero-free regions, zero density, or verification up to any height. The parent (generalized Riemann hypothesis, all Dirichlet L-functions) is not part of this bullet; this bullet is the zeta case.

events.what_happened: On 10 August 2026 Anthropic announced (blog post https://anthropic.com/research/riemann-zeta, updated 13 August 2026 'with an updated version of Claude's paper') a result found by an unreleased research version of Claude in two Claude Code sessions. The paper, arXiv:2608.13637 'More than two thirds of the zeta zeros are simple and on the critical line' by Levent Alpöge and Ralph Furman (Anthropic mathematicians), carries the title-block note 'The mathematical argument in this paper was discovered and written by Claude, an AI developed by Anthropic', and its arXiv comments field reads 'Proof discovered autonomously by Claude (Anthropic); verified and communicated by the listed authors.' It raises the unconditional share of nontrivial zeta zeros that are simple and on the line from 5/12 (≈41.7%, Pratt–Robles–Zaharescu–Zeindler, cited by the paper and the press as 41.6%) to at least 2/3, and the distinct-zero share to at least 5/6. A Lean 4 formalisation is at github.com/anthropics/formal-math (directory zeta23; also cited as anthropics/zeta-23-lean).
events.revisions: Anthropic post 10 Aug 2026, updated 13 Aug 2026 with an updated version of the paper; arXiv:2608.13637 v1 13 Aug 2026 (17:44 UTC), v2 19 Aug 2026 (18:17 UTC).
events.delivers: Unconditional lower bounds as T→∞ for zeros in [T,2T], counted with multiplicity: at least (2/3 − o(1))N(T,2T) are simple and lie on Re s = 1/2 (Theorem A(i)); at least (5/6 − o(1))N(T,2T) are distinct (Theorem A(ii)). With a Montgomery–Taylor window the constants become 0.6725 and 0.8362 (abstract; the theorem statement gives 0.83625). The paper says it does not assume RH and presents the argument as making Montgomery's 1973 deduction unconditional: the RH input is replaced by a rank-trace inequality on a finite compression of Weil's Hermitian form, with Sylvester's law of inertia handling off-line pairs, using analytic inputs from Aryan and from Baluyot–Goldston–Suriajaya–Turnage-Butterbaugh. Theorem E extends the bounds to primitive Dirichlet L-functions (stated in the paper; I did not check that part in detail).
events.remains: The statement that every nontrivial zero lies on the line. The theorem bounds the share of zeros in windows that are simple and on the line at 2/3, so at least 1/3 of zeros in [T,2T] are not controlled by it, and it says nothing about zeros off the line. Anthropic's own post: 'We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.'

events.what_happened: Youness Lamzouri posted 'A new proof that more than 2/3 of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are simple and on the critical line', giving 'a new, conceptually simpler, unconditional proof that more than 67.25% of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are simple and on the critical line' and at least 83.62% are distinct. The method replaces the finite-dimensional matrix framework of the Claude argument by a single Hilbert-space inequality. It also gives two estimates the Claude paper 'neither states nor proves': the proportion of zeros that are simple or on the line (or both) is at least 88.76%, and the average of the simple-on-line and on-line proportions is at least 83.62%. The abstract says the bounds 'were very recently produced by an internal research version of Claude developed by Anthropic and subsequently verified by two mathematicians at Anthropic'.
events.revisions: v1 2 Sep 2026 (17:56 UTC); v2 8 Sep 2026 (comments: 'We also expand the exposition').
events.delivers: The same unconditional kind of bound as event alpoge-furman-claude-2026-08, for zeros of the zeta function: more than 67.25% of nontrivial zeros simple and on the line, at least 83.62% distinct, by an independent route; plus the two estimates above (88.76% for simple-or-on-line; average 83.62%). The abstract states these for the Riemann zeta function; it does not claim anything for other Dirichlet L-functions.
events.remains: All nontrivial zeros on the line; the share of zeros not covered by these proportions (at least about one-third); simplicity of all zeros.

checked_by.what_they_did: Independent re-derivation of the 67.25% and 83.62% bounds by a different proof, which is a human check of the same quantity as event alpoge-furman-claude-2026-08; the paper does not state that it checks the Claude argument line by line

events.doubts: The paper does not say whether it is independent of the Claude argument or builds on it; the abstract says its approach replaces the Claude matrix framework, which suggests a distinct route, but this is an inference. No doubt about its correctness appears in any source I read.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture, in proportion; the same direction as event alpoge-furman-claude-2026-08.

events.what_happened: Biao Wang (sole author) posted 'Simple critical zeros and distinct zeros of the Riemann zeta-function in short intervals', which gives lower bounds on the number of nontrivial zeros in short intervals that are simple and on the critical line, and distinct, by using Lamzouri's method and a Montgomery pair-correlation theorem for short intervals (after Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh). It cites Lamzouri and Alpöge–Furman.
events.delivers: Lower bounds for simple-on-line and distinct zeros in short intervals; the abstract gives no explicit constants or interval lengths, so the strength of the bounds is not recorded here.
events.remains: The statement that all nontrivial zeros lie on the line, and the zero count in short intervals beyond the unstated constants.
events.doubts: Single-author preprint with no referee or expert reaction found. The abstract gives no numerical constants to compare with the Alpöge–Furman and Lamzouri figures.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture, in short-interval proportions; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Biao Wang posted 'Proportions of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function', claiming to refine the Lamzouri-method constants: C₀ = 3/2 − (1/√2)cot(1/√2) ≈ 0.67250 is refined to C₀ + δ₀, and C₁ = (C₀+1)/2 ≈ 0.83625 to C₁ + δ₀/2, with δ₀ ≈ 6.66624×10⁻⁸. The preprint was later withdrawn by its author.
events.revisions: v1 21 Sep 2026; v2 6 Oct 2026, carrying 'This paper has been withdrawn by Biao Wang'.
events.delivers: As the abstract states it, a refinement of the Alpöge–Furman constants by about 7×10⁻⁸. Withdrawn, so it establishes nothing that stands.
events.remains: Everything in the statement; the withdrawn preprint does not move the problem.
events.doubts: Withdrawn by the author on 6 Oct 2026. The page I read gives no reason for the withdrawal. The abstract's comment reads 'New method is need to obtain good improvement.'

withdrawn.what: Preprint arXiv:2609.24167 withdrawn by its author; v2 (6 Oct 2026) carries the withdrawal notice

events.direction: Toward the conjecture, in proportion, by a very small refinement; withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Andrew Pearce-Crump posted 'Optimising Selberg's method for critical zeros', whose abstract says it proves 'that at least 7% of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line' by optimising Selberg's method.
events.revisions: v1 14 Sep 2026 (10:17 UTC), the only version.
events.delivers: A positive proportion (at least 7%) of nontrivial zeros on the line, as the abstract states it. The abstract does not say whether the result is unconditional and does not relate it to the Alpöge–Furman bound.
events.remains: The statement that all nontrivial zeros lie on the line; the remaining proportion.
events.doubts: The 7% figure is far below the earlier unconditional record of about 41.7% (Pratt–Robles–Zaharescu–Zeindler) and the 67.25% figure of event alpoge-furman-claude-2026-08, so unless the paper proves a different quantity it does not move the record. The abstract does not say whether the result is new. A positive proportion from Selberg's method is classical (background knowledge, not checked in the sources here). The paper does not mention Claude, Anthropic or Lamzouri.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture, but only a positive proportion, and weaker than the existing record.

events.what_happened: Kristian Muri Knausgård posted 'More than 83.9% of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are distinct and more than 67.35% are simple and on the critical line', with Lean 4 proofs of lower bounds liminf N_d(T)/N(T) ≥ 1645064/1960733 ≈ 0.83900 (distinct) and liminf N₀ˢ(T)/N(T) ≥ 0.67353 (simple and on the line). The abstract says the proofs 'use three axioms beyond those of Mathlib, one per inequality', each of which 'records that a search program returned true; Lean's kernel does not check the run itself', and calls the work 'an experiment in AI-assisted mathematical research'. The abstract's text also gives '67.80%' in one sentence while the title gives 67.35%. Lean files and certificates are in the ancillary files.
events.revisions: v1 6 Oct 2026 only; 43 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables.
events.delivers: Lower bounds (liminf) for the distinct and simple-on-line proportions, slightly above the Alpöge–Furman constants (per the abstract). The Lean statements depend on three extra axioms standing for computer-search results that the kernel does not check, so the formal result is conditional on those three computational assertions.
events.remains: The statement that all zeros lie on the line; the remaining proportion; the three computational axioms are not discharged in Lean.

events.doubts: (a) Three extra axioms encode computer-search outputs that Lean does not check, so the Lean result is not a kernel-checked proof of the bounds. (b) The title says 67.35% and the abstract says 67.80% in one sentence. (c) Single author, no referee or expert engagement found.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture, in proportion; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published 722 manuscripts (372 families) from an unreleased internal model on the openai/math GitHub repository. Family 003 claims a zero-free half-plane: no zero of the Riemann zeta function or of any Dirichlet L-function has real part greater than 7/8, uniformly over all positive moduli and characters, with the principal-character pole at s = 1 excluded. The Lean docs state the formalisation 'claims θ = 7/8 for the Riemann zeta function and every Dirichlet L-function', and say the same bound holds for finite-order Hecke L-functions over Q(√−3). A companion manuscript gives Re s > 11/12 for zeta by a different proof, and a further file (SiegelZeros.lean) claims one constant c > 0 with real zeros of primitive real characters of conductor q ≥ 3 satisfying 1−β ≥ c/log q (no value of c given).
events.revisions: Catalogue posted 6 Oct 2026. No later revision seen in the pages I opened.
events.delivers: A zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for ζ(s) and all Dirichlet L-functions (uniform over moduli and characters; the principal-character pole excluded), a bound on the real parts of all nontrivial zeros; and, per the Lean docs, the same for finite-order Hecke L-functions over Q(√−3). The 11/12 companion (ζ only) is weaker. The Landau–Siegel statement gives a c/log q bound with c unspecified.
events.remains: The statement that every nontrivial zero of ζ has real part 1/2: the strip 1/2 < Re s ≤ 7/8 is not settled. The generalized Riemann hypothesis for all Dirichlet L-functions is likewise not settled. The Landau–Siegel constant is not explicit.
events.time_since_posted: 1 week; only reactions found, no verification

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (openai/math lean docs for family 003; files named in the docs: QuasiRiemannHypothesis.lean, DirichletSevenEighths.lean, HeckeSevenEighths.lean, SiegelZeros.lean)

events.doubts: (a) Unreviewed. The repository README says 'Not all have accompanying Lean formalizations' and 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues'; it says about 42% of top-line results are formalized. (b) I could not locate the four named Lean files in the lean/OAI folders I opened, so the sorry status and the fidelity of the Lean statement to the informal claim are unverified. (c) The claim is a uniform real-part bound for every Dirichlet L-function, far stronger than the zero-free regions known to me (background; secondary coverage quotes Kontorovich saying the known region gets thinner at larger heights). (d) It conflicts with the Kubalalika claim Θ = 1 (event kubalalika-2006-12546). (e) Secondary coverage reports Altman saying the results are not yet confirmed by outside mathematicians, and a reviewer saying they had not rerun the Lean library (search snippets; not opened). (f) The README's own count of manuscripts is 719 in 372 families, against 722 in press coverage.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture in form, but not the conjecture: a bound that places all zeros in Re s ≤ 7/8, which is consistent with RH and does not contradict it; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Vladimir Ryazanov posted 'A proof of the Riemann hypothesis on zeros of ζ-function' (arXiv:1808.10774, math.GM), using the Nyman–Beurling criterion. The listing is dated 30 Aug 2018 for v1; the title and claim then changed between versions: the v6 abstract (24 Jan 2025) says 'it is disproved the Riemann hypothesis', and v1 and the current version say it is proved. The current v11 abstract: 'In this preprint, applying the known Beurling–Nyman criterion, it is just proved the Riemann hypothesis.'
events.revisions: v1 30 Aug 2018 (proof claim); v2 3 Sep 2018; v3 8 Apr 2019; v4 11 Apr 2019; v5 10 Dec 2024; v6 24 Jan 2025 (retitled 'A disproof of the Riemann hypothesis on zeros of ζ-function'); v7 6 Jul 2025; v8 17 Jul 2025; v9 25 Jul 2025 (an HTML version titled 'A disproof of the Riemann hypothesis' appeared in search snippets, not opened); v10 25 Aug 2026; v11 31 Aug 2026 (current, 'A proof of the Riemann hypothesis').
events.delivers: On the author's stated claim: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis via the Nyman–Beurling criterion (v1, v11), or a disproof (v6). The two claims contradict each other.
events.remains: Nothing, on the claim as stated in v11; the versions contradict each other, so no single claim can be recorded as the event's content.
events.time_since_posted: about 8 years since v1; no engagement found
events.doubts: The version history flips between proof and disproof. The arXiv page shows math.GM; a PDF in search results gives an affiliation (Institute of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics, NASU), not verified on the arXiv page. No referee or specialist response found.
events.direction: Claims RH true in v1 and v11 and false in v6; contradictory across versions.

events.what_happened: Tatenda Kubalalika posted 'The Riemann Hypothesis is false' (arXiv:2006.12546), claiming Θ = 1, where Θ is the supremum of the real parts of the zeros of ζ, which the abstract says 'entails the existence of infinitely many Riemann zeros off the critical line'. The same paper was posted on Cambridge Engage on 13 Feb 2026 (not opened).
events.revisions: v1 16 Jun 2020; 49 versions, last v49 17 Feb 2026, which the author calls 'this shall be the very final revision'; addendum 11 Feb 2026 correcting a typo in v47. Search snippets (not opened) say some 2022 versions claimed Θ ≥ 3/4 and v8 (2022) claimed Θ = 1.
events.delivers: On the author's claim: Θ = 1, which disproves RH. The claim is a statement about the supremum of real parts, not an explicit zero off the line.
events.remains: Nothing, on the claim; the claim concerns the complement of RH.
events.time_since_posted: about 6 years since v1 (last revised 17 Feb 2026); no engagement found

events.doubts: Self-published, not submitted for review, and the author invites testing. The Lean build and axioms are not checked. A separate GitHub repository (codegod100/rh) is conditional and has sorry stubs (see dead_ends).
events.direction: Toward RH (claimed full proof).

events.what_happened: Pratt, Robles, Zaharescu and Zeindler, 'More than five-twelfths of the zeros of ζ are on the critical line', proving that at least 5/12 (about 41.67%) of nontrivial zeros are on the critical line unconditionally. Cited in the Alpöge–Furman paper as the previous unconditional record. Dated from a mirror of the arXiv listing (15 Sep 2019); Sugaku metadata gives 2018; later papers cite it as 2020. Not opened on arXiv.
events.revisions: Dates inconsistent across secondary sources (2018, 2019, 2020).
events.delivers: An unconditional lower bound of 5/12 for the proportion of nontrivial zeros on the critical line. Per a Goldston–Suriajaya summary (not opened), the same work gives at least 40.7% simple-and-on-line.
events.remains: All of RH and the stronger proportions later obtained.
events.time_since_posted: about 6 years; the result is cited as the previous record in later papers
events.doubts: None raised. Dated from secondary sources only.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture, in proportion; a partial result.

events.what_happened: Dave Platt and Tim Trudgian, 'The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3·10¹²' (arXiv:2004.09765), using rigorous interval arithmetic to verify that every zero with 0 < γ ≤ 3·10¹² has real part 1/2. A DOI on the arXiv page points to Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society (doi 10.1112/blms.12460; journal not opened).
events.revisions: v1 21 Apr 2020; journal version via DOI 10.1112/blms.12460 (not opened).
events.delivers: Verification of RH for all zeros with imaginary part at most 3·10¹² (height). It is a finite instance check, so it does not bear on the universal statement.
events.remains: Every zero above height 3·10¹², and the universal claim.
events.directly_checkable: Finite zero computation with interval arithmetic; the zeros can be checked numerically, not by hand.
events.doubts: None raised. The result covers only zeros up to height 3·10¹²; the paper does not cover whether zeros are simple.
events.direction: Consistent with RH up to the height; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Larry Guth and James Maynard, 'New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials' (arXiv:2405.20552), with a zero-density estimate N(σ,T) ≤ T^{30(1−σ)/13+o(1)}, where N(σ,T) counts zeros with real part above σ and imaginary part at most T, and an application to primes in short intervals of length x^{17/30+o(1)}. Per a Princeton Annals listing (search snippet, not opened), published in Annals of Mathematics (2026).
events.delivers: A zero-density bound for zeta: the number of zeros with real part above σ is at most T^{30(1−σ)/13+o(1)}. RH is equivalent to N(σ,T) = 0 for every σ > 1/2, so this moves a quantity the statement's question turns on, but it leaves the count positive for every σ > 1/2 and proves nothing about RH itself.
events.remains: The statement that N(σ,T) = 0 for every σ > 1/2, i.e. RH; the density bound is positive for σ > 1/2.

checked_by.who: Annals of Mathematics (journal of record, per a Princeton listing seen in search results)

events.doubts: None on the mathematics, which I did not check. The bound is for zeros with real part above σ and does not itself bear on RH, which requires zero counts for σ > 1/2 to vanish. Whether the published version matches v2 is not checked.
events.direction: Toward RH in the sense of bounding zeros off the line, but leaves the question open; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: Bin Chen, Vishal Gupta and Yung Chi Li, 'Large Value Estimates for Dirichlet Polynomials with Characters and Zero Density of Dirichlet L-Functions' (arXiv:2507.08296), giving a zero-density estimate for all L(s,χ) with χ mod q, summed over characters, with exponent 7/3 in Σ N(σ,T,χ) ≪ (qT)^{7(1−σ)/3+ε}, improving Huxley's 12/5.
events.delivers: A zero-density bound for the family of Dirichlet L-functions (all characters mod q, not only primitive). The principal character's L-function is ζ with finitely many Euler factors removed, so the bound touches the zeta case, but the abstract does not say so and does not mention ζ.
events.remains: RH for ζ and the generalized Riemann hypothesis for the family.
events.doubts: None raised; the bound is a density estimate and does not bear on RH directly. The principal-character point is my reading, not the abstract's.
events.direction: Neutral to RH: a zero-density bound for a family that includes the zeta case.

events.what_happened: ShiJie Wei, Yue Zhai, Quanfeng Lu and eight co-authors (including Franco Nori, Tao Xin, GuiLu Long), 'The Riemann Hypothesis Emerges in Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions' (arXiv:2511.11199, quant-ph), propose a 'direct correspondence' between the nontrivial zeros of ζ and dynamical quantum phase transitions, and claim to 'experimentally demonstrate this correspondence on a five-qubit spin-based system'.
events.revisions: v1 only, 14 Nov 2025.
events.delivers: A physical reformulation and an experiment; the abstract does not claim a proof of RH or an equivalence.
events.remains: The statement that every zero is on the line.
events.doubts: The abstract calls RH 'one of the most profound unsolved problems in mathematics' and does not claim a proof. The experiment is a numerical or physical check of a correspondence, not a check of RH at new heights. Read from the abstract only.
events.direction: Neutral to RH; a reformulation with no resolution.

events.what_happened: Alain Connes, 'The Riemann Hypothesis: Past, Present and a Letter Through Time' (arXiv:2602.04022), a 42-page survey of approaches to RH plus a three-page 'Letter to Riemann' that extremises a quadratic form built from primes below 13 and reports approximations to the first 50 zeros, with a general claim that these approximating values lie exactly on the critical line. The abstract says the results 'suggest a promising direction for future research on Riemann's conjecture'. A journal version is listed in Journal of Open Mathematical Problems (search snippet, not opened).
events.revisions: v1 only (3 Feb 2026); comments say it was submitted to JOMP on 19 Sep 2025.
events.delivers: A survey and a method for approximating zeros. The claim concerns the approximating values, not the zeros of ζ, so it does not establish that any zero lies on the line.
events.remains: The statement that all nontrivial zeros lie on the line.
events.time_since_posted: about 8 months; the Wikipedia lead cites it (key Connes2026); no mathematical verification found
events.directly_checkable: Approximations and their accuracies can be checked numerically from the stated quadratic form.
events.doubts: The abstract says the work proposes a direction, not a proof. The general claim about 'approximating values' is the author's, and I did not check it.
events.direction: Neutral to RH; a method and a survey; no claimed resolution.

events.what_happened: The same Kubalalika claim was posted on Cambridge Engage as 'The Riemann Hypothesis is false' (dated 13 Feb 2026) and labelled as not peer reviewed. Recorded here as a posting of the same claim, not a separate result. The Cambridge page was not opened; the posting date and label come from a search summary.
events.revisions: Posting of the arXiv v49 claim.
events.delivers: The same claim as kubalalika-2006-12546, Θ = 1.
events.remains: Nothing, on the claim.
events.doubts: Same as kubalalika-2006-12546.
events.direction: Against RH: claims Θ = 1.

events.what_happened: Daniel Goldston, Junghun Lee, Jordan Schettler and Ade Irma Suriajaya, 'Pair Correlation Conjecture for the zeros of the Riemann zeta-function II: The Alternative Hypothesis' (arXiv:2507.06823). The abstract says it formulates an Alternative Hypothesis giving a different pair-correlation conjecture, and under it 'asymptotically 100% of the zeros are both simple and on the critical line'; RH is not assumed, but the Alternative Hypothesis is.
events.revisions: v1 only, 9 Jul 2025 (14 KB).
events.delivers: Conditional on the Alternative Hypothesis (a pair-correlation variant), asymptotically all zeros are simple and on the line. Unconditionally, nothing about the line.
events.remains: The unconditional statement, and every zero, since the result depends on the unproven Alternative Hypothesis.
events.doubts: Conditional on a hypothesis that is itself open. The abstract does not state the hypothesis in full; I read the abstract only.
events.direction: Toward RH only conditionally, on a different conjecture.

events.what_happened: Daniel Goldston and Ade Irma Suriajaya, 'Zeta Zeros on the Critical Line' (arXiv:2511.20059), an expository note showing that if RH could be removed from Montgomery's simple-zero proof, the same argument would give that at least 2/3 of the zeros are simple and on the critical line. The Alpöge–Furman paper later states that its Theorem A is the removal of exactly this hypothesis.
events.delivers: A reduction: if RH could be removed from Montgomery's argument, 2/3 of zeros would be simple and on the line. It does not prove this.
events.remains: The removal of RH from Montgomery's argument (the step the Alpöge–Furman paper claims), and RH.
events.doubts: None raised by the authors. The Alpöge–Furman paper cites this note, so its claim to remove the RH hypothesis is directly connected; the later pass should compare the two.
events.direction: Reduction toward the conjecture in proportion; no resolution.

events.what_happened: Two manuscripts claim zero-free half-planes for zeta. 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis: A Zero-Free Half-Plane Re s>7/8' (Sept 30 2026) claims that every finite-order Hecke L-function over Q(√-3) and every Dirichlet L-function, zeta included, has no zero with Re s > 7/8, with the principal pole at s=1 allowed. Its Part I proves the same statement with 11/12 in place of 7/8 (Theorem 'The 11/12 half-plane'), and Part II builds on that. 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis' (Oct 5 2026) claims the weaker half-plane Re s > 11/12 for the same families, by a route through a mean-square bound for twisted Möbius sums; it describes the 7/8 result as stronger. For zeta, the claim is that every nontrivial zero has real part at most 7/8 (Sept 30) or at most 11/12 (Oct 5).
events.delivers: A fixed zero-free strip next to the line Re s = 1 for zeta: no nontrivial zero with real part in (7/8, 1) according to Sept 30, or in (11/12, 1) according to Oct 5. Zeros with 0 < Re s ≤ 7/8 (or ≤ 11/12) are not restricted to any line, so the location question is not decided. The Sept 30 introduction says that the theorem does not establish the Riemann hypothesis or its generalized versions.
events.remains: That every nontrivial zero of zeta with 0 < Re s ≤ 7/8 (or ≤ 11/12) has real part exactly 1/2. The list's universal claim is otherwise untouched.

machine_checked.scope:
The quasi-Riemann hypothesis asks for a fixed zero-free half-plane $\Re s>\theta$ with $\theta<1$. The formalization gives $\theta=7/8$ for the Riemann zeta function and every Dirichlet $L$-function, uniformly over all positive moduli and all characters. It also establishes the same bound for finite-order Hecke $L$-functions over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$.

The principal-character poles at $s=1$ are excluded in the Dirichlet and Hecke statements. The paper's later applications are not included.

The formalized result gives a uniform logarithmic exclusion region for Landau–Siegel zeros. There is one constant $c>0$ such that every primitive nonprincipal real Dirichlet character of conductor $q\ge3$ and every real zero $0<\beta<1$ of its $L$-function satisfy $1-\beta\ge c/\log q$.

Both character parities are included. No explicit value of $c$ is given. This excludes real zeros in $1-c/\log q<\beta<1$, but does not rule out real zeros elsewhere in $(0,1)$.

events.doubts: (1) The Sept 30 TeX is about 16,700 lines. I read the statements, the proof overview, the Part I/II transition, the final assembly and a few lemma statements, not the body. The argument is a contradiction (assume β* > 7/8) that depends on many declared hypotheses, some of which the text says are 'verified' later. Near line 5648 the text calls the high identity 'a hypothesis to be proved for the physical expression, not its definition'; I did not trace where that is discharged. (2) Oct 5 calls its outline a sketch that suppresses coprimality conditions, local factors and smoothing; the full argument is in later sections. I read the reduction and the proof of Proposition thm:ms, which reduces to Proposition 'canonical' and the iteration, but not the reflection, transfer or appendix sections. (3) The Oct 5 README says 'This paper was written with human assistance.' The Sept 30 and Oct 1 READMEs say no such thing.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis is stated. Some steps are taken from published work without proof here: the number-field quadratic large sieve of Goldmakher and Louvel, the cubic theta coefficient and transformation formulas of Patterson and Dunn–Radziwiłł, Heath-Brown's admissible-exponent method, and the Hecke functional equation. Sept 30's Part II depends on its own Part I, which it uses to get β* ≤ 11/12 and hence Δ ≤ 1/24. Oct 5 does not depend on Sept 30; its introduction cites Sept 30 only for the stronger 7/8 result.
events.direction: proves a zero-free half-plane (partial result toward RH, the quasi-RH)

disputes.summary: Press coverage says Brian Conrey and Dan Goldston reviewed or validated the Claude result. The paper thanks them for carefully reading the manuscript and for their comments, and the Anthropic post thanks them as experts. Neither is quoted endorsing the result, and no outside verification was found.

The arXiv listing and paper name Alpöge and Furman as authors, while the paper's title-block note says the argument was 'discovered and written by Claude'. The Anthropic post says Jarred Sumner posed the problem. Press coverage credits different parties.

The OpenAI family 003 claim places all zeros of ζ and all Dirichlet L-functions in Re s ≤ 7/8, while the Kubalalika claim (arXiv 2006.12546, v49 Feb 2026) says the supremum of real parts is 1. Both cannot hold; neither is refereed.

Ryazanov's arXiv 1808.10774 has been a proof claim (v1 2018; v11 Aug 2026) and a disproof claim (v6 Jan 2025, and an HTML version titled 'A disproof' in search results). The author has not withdrawn either.

Some press coverage of the OpenAI family 003 result says the model 'proved the Riemann hypothesis' (search snippets from KuCoin and 36Kr, not opened). The repository and the Lean docs state a zero-free half-plane at 7/8, which is the quasi-Riemann claim, not RH.

summary: No accepted resolution of the Riemann hypothesis, and no accepted partial result of it either, has appeared since 26 January 2024; the events found are partial proportion theorems, a claimed zero-free half-plane, reductions and conditional results, and many unrefereed claims of a full proof or disproof. The most substantial event is arXiv:2608.13637 (Alpöge and Furman, 10–13 August 2026), which the paper credits to an unreleased research version of Claude ('discovered and written by Claude'): an unconditional bound that at least two-thirds of zeros in windows [T,2T] are simple and on the line, with a Lean 4 formalisation that its README and paper describe as sorry-free (I did not rebuild it). Verification by humans is limited: the authors are Anthropic mathematicians, the acknowledged readers Conrey and Goldston are thanked for reading and commenting, not endorsing, and the paper names model instances as adversarial reviewers. Lamzouri's arXiv:2609.02882 (2 September 2026) is an independent, shorter human proof of the 67.25% bound and is the strongest human check so far; his abstract attributes the earlier bounds to Claude and does not credit Claude with the new proof, so I recorded none_found true for that event. The OpenAI family 003 result (6 October 2026) is a zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for ζ and all Dirichlet L-functions, with Lean docs whose sorry status I could not establish, and its AI attribution is to an unnamed internal model. It bounds where zeros can be, which is consistent with RH and does not settle it. Close calls: (1) whether the Alpöge–Furman bound 'moved a quantity the problem names' or 'settled a restricted case' — the statement is universal over zeros, the result bounds a proportion of zeros in windows; the bound moves the share of zeros on the line but leaves the universal claim untouched, which is the scope question for the judging pass. (2) Whether the Eureka Math/Conjecture Agent result (19 August 2026) is about RH: the abstract ties it to RH only through a localised Weil-form positivity constant and does not say what the constant implies. (3) Whether the Knausgård result (6 October 2026) is a Lean proof: it uses three extra axioms, one per inequality, each encoding a computer-search result the kernel does not check. The repository-level claims (Ryazanov, Kubalalika, Fayed, Nielsen–Semita, Artykbayev, Easwaran, Atiyah, the Zeta Resonator) are recorded as events with the evidence I could gather; none has expert engagement in the sources, and several are contradictory across their own versions. Pre-window background: the 5/12 record (Pratt et al.), the zero-density bounds of Guth–Maynard and Chen–Gupta–Li, and the 3·10¹² height verification (Platt–Trudgian) are recorded as events; the earlier proportion chain (Levinson, Conrey, Feng, Bui–Conrey–Young) is not recorded separately. The current Wikipedia lead (read in part) says there is 'overwhelming numerical evidence' and 'no proof is known', and that the Clay Institute offers US$1 million for a solution; it does not mention the 2026 proportion results in the portion I read.
competing_reading: Read the Alpöge–Furman result as a restricted case, not a movement of the problem's own quantity. The bullet asks about every nontrivial zero; the theorem bounds the share of zeros in windows that are simple and on the line, leaves at least a third of them uncontrolled, and says nothing about zeros off the line. On that reading the bullet has no resolution event, only partial proportion events, and the AI-credited bound is a bound event at most. The opposing reading: the bullet's content is the location of zeros, and a lower bound on the share on the line is a direct move in the quantity that location is measured by (compare the zero-density bound of Guth–Maynard, which moves the count of zeros with Re > σ). On that reading the Claude-credited result is a bound event with AI involvement that the later pass must weigh, and the judging pass decides which side governs.
what_would_settle_it: For event alpoge-furman-claude-2026-08: a referee report or journal acceptance of arXiv:2608.13637, or a written verification by an outside number theorist, and a rebuild of the Lean project (anthropics/formal-math/zeta23) confirming the '#print axioms' output and that Theorems A–E match the paper; also resolution of the 'EnclOK' displayed hypothesis in the PairCeiling section. For openai-family-003-quasi-rh-2026-10: the QuasiRiemannHypothesis.lean file located, built, and its sorry status checked, plus an expert check that the formal 7/8 statement matches the informal claim and an outside referee report. For knausgard-2610-08965: a search-free Lean proof of the three axioms. For ryazanov-1808-10774 and kubalalika-2006-12546: a specialist's written verdict, or a withdrawal. For the whole question: a survey or database entry (for example the Breakthrough Tracker, not opened) recording the status of the Alpöge–Furman bound after refereeing.

incomplete: (1) The Anthropic PDFs and the arXiv PDF of 2608.13637 were unreadable through the fetch tool; the provenance, Appendix B, Lean and acknowledgment content come from the arXiv HTML rendering, read in two fetches. The Lean code itself was not read or rebuilt; the sorry and axiom statements are the paper's and the README's. (2) The Live Science article was not readable; the Maynard and Sutherland quotes are from a search snippet. event.what_happened: Larry Guth and James Maynard, 'New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials' (arXiv:2405.20552), with a zero-density estimate N(σ,T) ≤ T^{30(1−σ)/13+o(1)}, where N(σ,T) counts zeros with real part above σ and imaginary part at most T, and an application to primes in short intervals of length x^{17/30+o(1)}. Per a Princeton Annals listing (search snippet, not opened), published in Annals of Mathematics (2026).
event.delivers: A zero-density bound for zeta: the number of zeros with real part above σ is at most T^{30(1−σ)/13+o(1)}. RH is equivalent to N(σ,T) = 0 for every σ > 1/2, so this moves a quantity the statement's question turns on, but it leaves the count positive for every σ > 1/2 and proves nothing about RH itself.
event.remains: The statement that N(σ,T) = 0 for every σ > 1/2, i.e. RH; the density bound is positive for σ > 1/2.

checked_by.who: Annals of Mathematics (journal of record, per a Princeton listing seen in search results)

event.doubts: None on the mathematics, which I did not check. The bound is for zeros with real part above σ and does not itself bear on RH, which requires zero counts for σ > 1/2 to vanish. Whether the published version matches v2 is not checked.
event.direction: Toward RH in the sense of bounding zeros off the line, but leaves the question open; no counterexample.

judgement.why: The statement is universal over zeros, so every proportion result (Alpöge–Furman/Claude 2/3, Lamzouri 67.25%, Knausgård), zero-density estimate (Guth–Maynard) and zero-free half-plane (OpenAI 7/8, which moves the supremum of real parts from 1) is a bound, not a case: none settles a restriction of the question. Alpöge–Furman is unreviewed: the verifiers are its own authors and AI instances, Conrey and Goldston are only thanked for reading, and Lamzouri re-proved the bound rather than reading the argument; its AI role is generated per the title-block note. Lamzouri is credible and human. Wang's short-interval bounds and Chen–Gupta–Li's family density estimate are different quantities (variant); Wang's refinement is withdrawn; Pearce-Crump's 7% is below the existing record so moves nothing. Reductions, conditional results, surveys and the Eureka constant are none. The full proof/disproof claims (Ryazanov, Kubalalika x2, Fayed, Nielsen–Semita, Artykbayev, Easwaran, Atiyah, Zeta Resonator) combine no uptake on a landmark problem with self-undermining histories and are not_credible. The two OpenAI rows describe the same family-003 claim; both are answered identically as generated, doubtful bounds.
judgement.doubts: openai-family-003-quasi-rh-2026-10 and openai-math-003 are the same event recorded twice. The OpenAI AI-role quotes are thin (compute statement; an 'exception to the fixed procedure' for the zeta zero-free region, plus an Oct 5 README saying 'written with human assistance'), so assisted is a defensible alternative to generated; generated chosen because the repository presents the manuscripts as the model's output. Guth–Maynard's 'digested' rests on an unopened Annals listing snippet. Pratt et al. left unreviewed for lack of a recorded journal.
